\title{Steam on the Loom: The Diffusion of Steam Power in the Cotton Mills of the Nord, 1830--1880}
\author{C.~Deveraux}
\date{January 2026}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
This article traces the adoption of steam power in the cotton spinning
and weaving mills of the Nord department between 1830 and 1880. Drawing
on the industrial surveys of the statistical bureaus, on notarial records
of engine purchases, and on the archives of three machine builders in
Lille, it reconstructs the timing and geography of diffusion at the level
of individual communes. The evidence shows that steam displaced water
power in spinning two decades before it penetrated weaving, that adoption
clustered along the coal canal rather than along the rivers that had
powered the first mills, and that the decisive constraint was not the
price of engines but the supply of skilled enginemen.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
The mechanisation of the French cotton industry is usually told as a
story of lagging behind Britain, and the Nord is usually cast as the
exception that proves the rule: a region close to Belgian technology,
rich in coal, and quick to imitate. Yet the timing of steam adoption
within the Nord itself has never been mapped with any precision, and the
standard account rests on aggregate departmental statistics that conceal
sharp differences between communes and between branches of the trade.

This article reconstructs the diffusion process from below. Instead of
asking when the department as a whole adopted steam, it asks which mills
adopted, in which communes, in which branch of production, and with what
source of power before and after adoption. The answers complicate the
regional-success story in three ways: adoption was slower than the
aggregate series suggest, it was far more uneven geographically than the
canal-and-coal explanation implies, and it was organised around a
constraint, the supply of enginemen, that the literature has overlooked.

The argument proceeds in five steps. Section 2 sets out the sources and
the method of reconstruction. Section 3 describes the geography of water
power on the eve of steam. Section 4 traces the engine purchases
themselves. Section 5 examines the labour constraint, and Section 6
considers the weaving branch, where steam arrived last. Section 7
concludes with the implications for the comparative history of
continental industrialisation.

\section{Sources and Method}
Three bodies of evidence underpin the reconstruction. The first is the
series of industrial surveys conducted by the departmental statistical
bureau in 1838, 1852, 1861, and 1872, which report for each commune the
number of mills, the number and horsepower of steam engines, and the
number of water wheels. The second is the notarial archive of the
arrondissements of Lille, Roubaix, and Valenciennes, which preserves the
contracts of sale for engines and boilers, often with the maker's name,
the price, and the terms of credit. The third is the order books of three
machine builders active in Lille between 1835 and 1875, which record the
buyer, the destination, and the rated power of each engine delivered.

The three sources cross-check one another. Where the survey reports an
engine in a commune and the notarial archive preserves the contract, the
horsepower figures agree within ten percent in four cases out of five.
Where they disagree, the contract is preferred, on the ground that the
survey enumerators occasionally recorded rated rather than effective
power. The order books fill the gap between surveys and allow the dating
of adoption to the year rather than the survey period.

A mill is coded as an adopter in the year its first engine entered
service, whether or not it retained water power alongside. This
convention understates the completeness of the transition, since many
mills ran mixed systems for a decade or more, but it avoids the
arbitrariness of thresholds and matches the question of diffusion, which
is about the first commitment to the new technology.

\section{The Hydraulic Inheritance}
On the eve of the steam era the cotton mills of the Nord drew their power
from a handful of small rivers, above all the Marque and the De\^ule,
whose modest and irregular flow limited both the size and the location of
mills. The typical water-powered spinning mill of 1830 carried no more
than four thousand spindles, and its site was dictated by the fall of the
river rather than by the supply of labour or the price of land.

The hydraulic inheritance shaped the diffusion of steam in two opposing
ways. On one hand, the rivers had fixed the geography of the industry:
the workforce, the merchants, and the machine shops of 1830 were all
located along the valleys, and steam engines were at first installed in
existing water-powered sites as auxiliary power. On the other hand, the
scarcity of good hydraulic sites had capped the growth of the valleys,
and steam freed the industry to relocate toward the canal that carried
coal from the coalfield to the cities.

The interplay of these two forces explains the paradox at the heart of
this article: the canal corridor adopted steam earliest and most
completely, yet the river valleys did not decline, because their mills
were precisely the ones best placed to hybridise, running the wheel when
water was abundant and the engine when it was not.

\section{The Engine Purchases}
The notarial record preserves 212 contracts for the purchase of steam
engines by cotton mills between 1830 and 1880. The annual series shows a
slow start in the 1830s, a first wave between 1842 and 1848, a collapse
during the revolutionary years, and a sustained boom from 1855 to the end
of the period. The median engine grew from 12 horsepower in the first
wave to 40 horsepower in the boom, and the share of engines bought on
credit from the builder rose from a third to two thirds.

The geography of the purchases confirms the canal story with precision.
The communes along the coal canal account for 58 percent of all engines
bought before 1860, although they held barely 30 percent of the mills in
1830. The river communes of the Marque valley account for 22 percent, and
the remainder is scattered among the weaving towns and the smaller
centres of the countryside.

The order books of the Lille builders reveal a striking concentration of
supply. Before 1850, four mills in five that adopted steam bought their
engine from one of the three Lille shops or from a Belgian maker across
the border; after 1850 the Parisian builders entered the market, but the
Lille shops retained half of the departmental trade. Proximity to the
builder mattered less for the price than for the maintenance contract,
which the mills valued because their own enginemen were scarce and
expensive to replace.

\section{The Labour Constraint}
Every stage of the evidence points to the supply of skilled enginemen as
the binding constraint on adoption. The surveys report the wage of
enginemen at twice the wage of the best-paid spinners, and the notarial
archive preserves apprenticeship contracts that bound boys to engine
builders for six years. Mill owners' correspondence complains of
enginemen poached by rivals, of engines idle for want of a man to tend
them, and of the necessity of retaining a builder's mechanic on call at
an annual fee.

The constraint operated asymmetrically across the industry. Large mills
could spread the engineman's wage over many spindles and could train
their own men through apprenticeship; small mills could do neither, and
they responded in two ways. Some formed syndicates that shared an
engineman among three or four neighbouring mills, an arrangement whose
contracts survive in the notarial record. Others delayed adoption until
the builders offered maintenance contracts that substituted for a
resident engineman, which they did systematically only after 1855.

The dating of the second adoption wave supports this reading. The boom of
1855--1880 coincides almost exactly with the spread of the maintenance
contract, and the mills that adopted in the boom were on average half the
size of the mills that had adopted in the first wave. The fall in engine
prices, which the standard account credits with the boom, was real but
gradual; the abrupt change was the reallocation of the engineman's cost
from the mill to the builder.

\section{The Laggard Branch: Weaving}
Weaving adopted steam a full generation after spinning, and the delay
requires an explanation of its own. The technical reason usually given,
that the early power loom required a steadier motion than the small
engines of the 1830s could deliver, is undermined by the Belgian
evidence, where steam weaving was already common in the 1840s. The
French evidence suggests instead an organisational explanation: weaving
was conducted in small workshops and in rural putting-out, whose scale
could not support either an engine or an engineman.

The surveys trace the transition with unusual clarity. In 1852, fewer
than one weaving shed in ten in the department had steam power; in 1872,
the share had risen to one half, and the new steam sheds were
overwhelmingly located in the canal communes and organised as integrated
mills combining spinning and weaving under one roof. The rise of the
integrated mill, not the improvement of the loom, was the real carrier of
steam into the weaving branch.

The consequences for the rural handloom weavers were severe, and the
article closes its account of diffusion with their displacement: the
communes that adopted steam weaving last are the same communes whose
handloom population collapsed fastest in the census of 1876, a reminder
that the geography of adoption was also a geography of displacement.

\section{Conclusion}
The diffusion of steam power in the cotton mills of the Nord was slower,
more uneven, and more organisational than the aggregate statistics
suggest. Adoption clustered along the coal canal not simply because coal
was cheap there, but because the canal communes were where the machine
builders, the maintenance contracts, and the enginemen were. The
constraint that governed the pace of diffusion was human before it was
financial: mills adopted when they could secure the skills to run the
engine, whether by hiring, by sharing, or by contracting the skill away
to the builder. The comparative lesson is that the technology of the
first industrial revolution diffused through markets for skill as much as
through markets for machines, and that the geography of those skill
markets deserves a larger place in the history of continental
industrialisation than it has received.
\end{document}
